name: Hemiphileurus illatus
intro: I started with one male and two females from Arizona. I housed them the way I had kept Phileurus valgus. Within twelve days I found eggs in one female’s substrate, and by winter I could follow the brood into its pupal cells.

facts.title: Eggs found
facts.text: August 5, in the substrate of one female

sections.title: Starting with a trio
sections.text: I set up the trio on July 24, 2013. When I checked one female’s substrate on August 5, I found eggs. If I were repeating the trial, I would keep each female’s laying material together through the first inspection. The twelve days describe the interval between two checks. The female may have laid well before I discovered the eggs.

sections.title: Using the comparison with Phileurus valgus
sections.text: My starting point was my Phileurus valgus method. For valgus I fill a 32 oz (about 950 mL) container about three-quarters full for each female, then move the eggs into a larger rearing box at a monthly check. I used comparable conditions for H. illatus. This group already had eggs when I checked well before the end of the first month.

sections.title: A brood through the winter
sections.text: By September 11 the earliest batch had reached the third instar. On November 7 all 25 larvae I was following were still alive. On February 21, 2014, about four out of five had made cells and I could already see pupae. I leave closed cells intact when checking a mixed group. Some larvae may still be feeding while their siblings have settled into chambers against the wall.
